---
title: "Stability landscapes of engagement (experimental)"
---

```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 10, fig.height = 6, dpi = 110,
                      comment = "#>")
options(width = 100)
library(Nestimate)
```

*Experimental.* `stability_landscape()`, `landscape_trend()` and
`landscape_surface()` are new in Nestimate 1.0.1; their arguments and
output may change in later releases.

Which engagement states are stable, which are easy to leave, and do
students with different trajectories live in different landscapes? A
stability landscape answers these questions by drawing the transition
network as a ball in a set of cups (Scheffer et al. 2009). The depth of a
cup is how long students stay in the state once they are there: a deep cup
holds the ball, a shallow one lets it roll out at the next step.

The data are `trajectories`: the engagement state of 138 students in each of
15 consecutive courses, coded `Disengaged`, `Average` or `Active`. A missing
value marks a course the student did not take; most missing values are
trailing runs, students who left the program.

```{r data}
head(trajectories)
```

The three states have a natural order, and the landscapes below are drawn
in it.

```{r states}
engagement <- c("Disengaged", "Average", "Active")
```

# The landscape of all students

## How stable is each engagement state?

`build_network()` estimates the transition network, the probability of
moving from each state to each other state between consecutive courses.
`stability_landscape()` turns it into a landscape. A state that is
followed by itself with probability $P_{ii}$ is left after
$1 / (1 - P_{ii})$ courses on average, its expected stay, and the depth of
its cup is the log of that stay, $-\log(1 - P_{ii})$. Expected stay is then
$e^{\text{depth}}$, the escape-time law of a particle in a potential well
(Kramers 1940); a state that is always left at once has depth 0. The
intervals come from 1000 resamples of students.

```{r landscape}
network <- build_network(trajectories, method = "relative")
landscape <- stability_landscape(network, states = engagement, iter = 1000,
                                 seed = 2026)
landscape
```

The table gives each cup's depth with its interval, the expected stay
(`dwell`), the stay probability and the share of observed courses spent in
the state. Active is the deepest cup (depth 1.20 [1.02, 1.38]): students
stay 3.3 courses on average once they are active. Average follows (0.94,
2.6 courses) and Disengaged is the shallowest (0.66, 1.9 courses). The
intervals of Active and Disengaged do not overlap. How deep a cup is and how
much time is spent in it are different things: Average holds 43% of the
courses against 38% for Active, because students enter Average more often,
but they leave it sooner.

With three states the chain also has a net circulation, the part of the
dynamics a landscape cannot show (Schnakenberg 1976): 0.009 per course
[0.003, 0.016], running
Active to Average to Disengaged and back to Active. Students decline one
step at a time and recover by the direct jump more often than the reverse.

```{r landscape-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(landscape)
```

The ball sits at the bottom of each cup; the grey bars are the 95%
intervals, and the right axis reads the depth as an expected stay. Under
each cup are its expected stay, its share of courses and where students go
when they leave it. Disengaged is shallow and drains towards Average (40% of
disengaged courses are followed by an average one, 12% by an active one).
Active is deep and, when left, is left for Average (27%) rather than for
Disengaged (3%).

# Trajectory clusters

## Do the students follow distinct trajectories?

`build_clusters()` groups the sequences by their Hamming distance with
partitioning around medoids, here into three clusters.

```{r clusters}
clusters <- build_clusters(trajectories, k = 3, seed = 2026)
clusters
```

The three clusters hold 47, 74 and 17 students, with an average silhouette
of 0.36, a moderate separation. `build_network()` on the clustering gives
one transition network per cluster, and `state_distribution()` describes
what each cluster consists of.

```{r cluster-states}
cluster_networks <- build_network(clusters)
state_distribution(cluster_networks)
```

Cluster 1 is mostly active (75% of its observed courses), cluster 2 mostly
average (60%, with 24% disengaged), and cluster 3 mostly disengaged (80%).
Cluster 3 also has little data: 70 observed courses for 17 students, out of
255 possible, because most of its students left the program early.

## What landscape does each cluster live in?

The same call on the grouped networks gives one landscape per cluster.

```{r cluster-landscape}
cluster_landscape <- stability_landscape(cluster_networks, states = engagement,
                                         iter = 1000, seed = 2026)
cluster_landscape
```

```{r cluster-landscape-plot, fig.height = 11}
plot(cluster_landscape)
```

The three clusters live in three different landscapes, each with one deep
cup.

- **Cluster 1** has its deep cup at Active (depth 1.63 [1.39, 1.89], 5.1
  courses per stay). Average and Disengaged are equally shallow (0.35 and
  0.39, under 1.5 courses per stay), and both drain towards Active: 62% of
  average courses and 47% of disengaged courses are followed by an active
  one. The net circulation is indistinguishable from zero (0.004
  [-0.004, 0.014]).
- **Cluster 2** has its deep cup at Average (1.12 [0.98, 1.25], 3.1 courses
  per stay). Active is as shallow as Disengaged (0.45 and 0.56), and 58% of
  active courses are followed by an average one. The circulation is clear
  of zero (0.014 [0.005, 0.024]): decline one step at a time, recovery by
  the direct jump.
- **Cluster 3** has its deep cup at Disengaged (2.20 [1.65, 2.74], 9.0
  courses per stay). Its other cups rest on very few transitions, 2 of them
  out of Active, so their intervals are wide: [0.00, 1.95] for Average and
  [0.00, Inf] for Active, an upper limit that is unbounded because Active is
  never left in some resamples. Only the Disengaged cup of this cluster is
  estimated with any precision.

## How long does it take to reach engagement in each cluster?

The landscape shows how stable each state is. The mean first passage time
from `passage_time()` turns this into time: the expected number of courses
to reach one state from another for the first time (Kemeny and Snell 1976).

```{r passage}
passage_time(cluster_networks, states = engagement)
```

From Disengaged, a cluster 1 student reaches Active in 2.0 courses on
average, a cluster 2 student in 9.1 and a cluster 3 student in 44, far
beyond the 15 courses of the program. In the other direction, Active to
Disengaged takes 26.1 courses in cluster 1, 6.7 in cluster 2 and 2.0 in
cluster 3. The cups of the landscape are the reason: in cluster 1 every road
leads back to Active, in cluster 3 every road leads to Disengaged.

# The landscape across the program

## Does the stability of each state change over the program?

`landscape_trend()` estimates the cup depths in a sliding window of five
courses (courses 1-5, 2-6, ..., 11-15) and draws one line per state, with
intervals from resampling students. The program phase is not derived from
the transitions, so the line shows how stability changes over time, not who
was selected.

```{r trend}
phase_trend <- landscape_trend(network, along = "phase", states = engagement,
                               iter = 500, seed = 2026)
phase_trend
```

```{r trend-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(phase_trend)
```

The order of the cups holds over the whole program: Active is the deepest
in every window (between 1.03 and 1.32, a stay of about three courses),
Average is second and Disengaged the shallowest. Disengaged changes the
most: its depth falls from 0.72 in courses 1-5 to 0.42 in courses 6-10 and
rises to 1.01 in courses 10-14, so disengagement holds students longest
near the end of the program.

## Does it change differently in each cluster?

```{r cluster-trend, fig.height = 10}
cluster_trend <- landscape_trend(cluster_networks, along = "phase",
                                 states = engagement, iter = 500, seed = 2026)
cluster_trend
plot(cluster_trend)
```

In cluster 1, Active is the deep cup in every window (1.45 to 1.89), and
the Disengaged cup disappears over the program: from 0.69 in courses 1-5 to
0 in the last windows, where every disengaged course is followed by a
different state. In cluster 2, Average stays the deep cup and deepens at
the end (1.17 to 1.38), and Disengaged becomes stickier (0.53 to 0.86).
Cluster 3 runs out of data: its students leave the program, so its later
windows have no Average or Active courses, and in some windows its
Disengaged cup is never left (21 such points across the three clusters,
left out of the lines).

## How does the landscape itself move over the program?

The same windows, with the cups and ridges of the stationary distribution
(`depth = "occupancy"`), drawn as a 3D landscape: the states run across,
the program runs into the picture, and each cup becomes a channel. Here a
cup sits at $-\log \pi$, lower when students spend more of the window in
the state, and a ridge at $-\log$ of the probability flux between two
states, higher when the switch is rarer (Wang et al. 2008). The windows
are six courses long.

```{r occupancy-surface, fig.width = 8, fig.height = 6.5}
occupancy_trend <- landscape_trend(network, along = "phase",
                                   depth = "occupancy", window = 6,
                                   states = engagement, iter = 500,
                                   seed = 2026)
occupancy_trend
plot(occupancy_trend, type = "surface")
```

For all students the landscape barely moves over the program. Average is
the lowest channel in every window (0.79 to 0.86), Active a little higher
(0.89 to 1.08) and Disengaged the highest (1.54 to 1.79).

```{r cluster-occupancy-surface, fig.width = 16, fig.height = 6}
cluster_occupancy <- landscape_trend(cluster_networks, along = "phase",
                                     depth = "occupancy", window = 6,
                                     states = engagement, iter = 500,
                                     seed = 2026)
cluster_occupancy
plot(cluster_occupancy, type = "surface")
```

The clusters' channels are steady too, but at different states. In cluster
1 the Active channel stays low throughout (0.26 to 0.35) while the
Disengaged ground rises from 2.44 to 3.84: disengagement becomes rarer as
the program goes on. In cluster 2 the Average channel stays low (0.45 to
0.54) and Active stays high (1.76 to 2.09). Cluster 3 can be drawn only in
its first window: after that its students are disengaged or gone, and the
chain of a window has no stationary distribution.

# Landscapes across stability measures

## Which cup deepens as students become more stable?

`landscape_surface()` adds a second axis: a per-student stability measure
from `sequence_metrics()`. At each value of the measure it computes the cup
depths from the 30 students closest to that value, weighted by a tricube
kernel (Cleveland 1979), so the surface runs from the most stable students
to the most volatile; the plot puts the most stable end in front. Six
measures are used: self-loop tendency (the share of courses that repeat the
previous state), longitudinal entropy, the complexity index, the longest
spell, cyclic feedback (how often a state recurs two or more courses later)
and initial-state persistence (the length of the opening spell).

```{r surface}
surface <- landscape_surface(network, states = engagement,
                             measure = c("self_loop_tendency",
                                         "longitudinal_entropy",
                                         "complexity_index",
                                         "max_spell_duration",
                                         "cyclic_feedback_strength",
                                         "initial_state_persistence"))
surface
```

```{r surface-plot, fig.width = 15, fig.height = 10}
plot(surface, ncol = 3)
```

Five of the six measures give the same answer. At the stable end every cup
deepens and Active is the deepest, between 2.94 and 3.18 on all five
measures, an expected stay of about 20 courses. Disengaged is the second
deepest for self-loop tendency, entropy and complexity (1.95 to 2.46, 7 to
12 courses): the most stable students are either stably active or, fewer of
them, stably disengaged. At the volatile end all three cups are shallow and
of similar depth (0.14 to 0.90), so no state holds the most volatile
students for more than about two and a half courses. Cyclic feedback
differs: as recurrence rises, the Active cup deepens (0.63 to 1.23) and the
Disengaged cup becomes shallower (0.99 to 0.54).

These measures come from the same sequences as the depths, so the cups of
the most stable students are deep by construction, self-loop tendency most
of all. What the surface adds is which cup deepens as stability rises:
Active first, Disengaged second.

## Does the same hold inside each cluster?

The same call on the clusters, with two measures: self-loop tendency and
longitudinal entropy.

```{r cluster-surface, warning = TRUE}
cluster_surface <- landscape_surface(cluster_networks, states = engagement,
                                     measure = c("self_loop_tendency",
                                                 "longitudinal_entropy"))
cluster_surface
```

```{r cluster-surface-plot, fig.width = 11, fig.height = 14}
plot(cluster_surface)
```

Within clusters, stability deepens the cluster's own cup. In cluster 1 the
Active cup deepens from 0.91 for the students with the lowest self-loop
tendency to 2.86 for the highest, and it is the deepest cup in every slice
of both measures. In cluster 2 the Average cup deepens from 0.62 to 1.92:
the most stable cluster 2 students are stably average, not stably active.
Cluster 3 has 4 to 8 effective students per slice, so its surfaces show no
more than its deep Disengaged cup.

# When to use which

| Question | Method |
|----------|--------|
| How long do students stay in each state, and where do they go when they leave? | `stability_landscape()` on a transition network |
| Do subgroups live in different landscapes? | `stability_landscape()` on a grouped network (`build_network()` of `build_clusters()`, or `group =`) |
| How long does it take to reach a state? | `passage_time()` |
| Does the stability of each state change over the program, or with a covariate such as a grade? | `landscape_trend()` (`along = "phase"` or a covariate) |
| Which state becomes the attractor as sequences become more stable? | `landscape_surface()` with a `sequence_metrics()` measure |

Run `stability_landscape()` first: it gives each state's depth with an
interval, its exits, and the net circulation, the part of the dynamics a
landscape leaves out. Add `passage_time()` when the question is about time. Use
`landscape_surface()` to ask which cup the stable sequences fall into, with
the full sample or large clusters; a cluster whose slices rest on fewer than
about ten effective sequences is too small for it.

# References

Cleveland, W. S. (1979). Robust locally weighted regression and smoothing
scatterplots. *Journal of the American Statistical Association*, 74,
829--836.

Kemeny, J. G., & Snell, J. L. (1976). *Finite Markov chains*. Springer.

Kramers, H. A. (1940). Brownian motion in a field of force and the diffusion
model of chemical reactions. *Physica*, 7, 284--304.

Scheffer, M., Bascompte, J., Brock, W. A., et al. (2009). Early-warning
signals for critical transitions. *Nature*, 461, 53--59.

Schnakenberg, J. (1976). Network theory of microscopic and macroscopic
behavior of master equation systems. *Reviews of Modern Physics*, 48,
571--585.

Wang, J., Xu, L., & Wang, E. (2008). Potential landscape and flux framework
of nonequilibrium networks. *PNAS*, 105, 12271--12276.
